proofs.proof_tex:
Write each comparison in the form
\[
 z_c-z_d<w_e(\kappa),
\]
where the corresponding directed edge is \(e=(d,c)\) and \(w_e(\kappa)\) is its weight in \(G_{\kappa,f}\).  If these inequalities have a solution, summing them around any directed cycle \(C\) gives
\[
 0=\sum_{e=(d,c)\in C}(z_c-z_d)<\sum_{e\in C}w_e(\kappa),
\]
so every directed simple cycle has strictly positive weight.

Conversely, suppose every directed simple cycle has positive weight.  The graph is finite because \(D\), \(M_1\), and \(M_2\) are finite.  If it has a directed cycle, choose
\[
 0<\delta<\min_C\frac{\sum_{e\in C}w_e(\kappa)}{|C|},
\]
where the minimum ranges over its finitely many directed simple cycles.  If it has no directed cycle, choose any \(\delta>0\).  Give edge \(e\) the modified weight \(\widetilde w_e=w_e(\kappa)-\delta\).  Every closed directed walk decomposes into directed simple cycles, and hence has nonnegative modified weight; in the acyclic case there is no closed directed walk.  Adjoin a source with a zero-weight edge to every vertex and let \(z_d\) be the minimum modified weight of a directed source-to-\(d\) path.  A minimum exists because deleting a nonnegative closed subwalk never increases path weight.  For every edge \((d,c)\),
\[
 z_c\le z_d+\widetilde w_{(d,c)}=z_d+w_{(d,c)}(\kappa)-\delta<z_d+w_{(d,c)}(\kappa).
\]
Thus \(z\) satisfies every strict comparison in the definition of \(F_\kappa\).  This proves \(f\in F_\kappa\) if and only if all simple-cycle weights are positive.

Finally, at a feasible \(z\) let
\[
 \gamma=\min_{e=(d,c)}\{w_e(\kappa)-(z_c-z_d)\}>0
\]
when there are edges.  Every \(z'\) with \(\|z'-z\|_\infty<\gamma/4\) changes any difference \(z_c-z_d\) by less than \(\gamma/2\), so it satisfies all comparisons strictly.  Hence an open axis-aligned cube lies in the patch.  If there are no edges, every \(z\in\mathbb R^J\) is feasible and the conclusion is immediate.  This also covers singleton menus.

Fix \(\kappa\).  Outside the finite union of utility-tie hyperplanes, a one-period total nonprice utility draw \(z\) determines exactly one response table \(f(z)\): it determines the first-period maximizer and, for every \(a\in M_1\), the second-period maximizer under lag \(a\).  By absolute continuity, conditional on each value of \(\lambda\) these hyperplanes have probability zero.  Define
\[
 q_f(\lambda)=\Pr\{f(\lambda+\epsilon_t)=f\mid\lambda\},\qquad f\in F_\kappa.
\]
Conditional time homogeneity makes this definition independent of \(t\), and the probabilities sum to one.  Conditional independence then gives, for every \(a\in M_1\) and \(b\in M_2\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr(Y_1=a,Y_2=b\mid\lambda)
 &=\Pr\{f_1(\lambda+\epsilon_1)=a\mid\lambda\}
   \Pr\{f_2(a;\lambda+\epsilon_2)=b\mid\lambda\}\\
 &=r_a(q(\lambda))s_{ab}(q(\lambda))
 =v_{ab}(q(\lambda)).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The first equality uses the utility index and maximization assumptions as well as conditional independence.  Integrating over \(\lambda\),
\[
 P=\int v(q(\lambda))\,dF_\lambda(\lambda).
\]
The simplex \(\Delta(F_\kappa)\) is compact and \(v\) is continuous, so its image is compact.  Its convex hull is compact as well: any convex combination with more than \(m\) points in the affine hyperplane \(\{x:\sum_{a,b}x_{ab}=1\}\) has an affine dependence, along which one can move the weights until one vanishes; repeating leaves at most \(m\) points.  Thus the convex hull is the continuous image of the compact set consisting of at most \(m\) points and their mixing weights.  Approximating the preceding integral by finite simple-function integrals and using closedness shows
\[
 P\in\operatorname{conv}\{v(q):q\in\Delta(F_\kappa)\}=\mathcal C_\kappa.
\]
This proves necessity and compactness.

For sufficiency, take \(P\in\mathcal C_\kappa\).  The same affine-dependence argument supplies
\[
 P=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_0}\omega_\ell v(q^\ell),
 \qquad 1\le L_0\le m,
 \qquad \omega_\ell\ge0,
 \qquad \sum_{\ell=1}^{L_0}\omega_\ell=1.
\]
For each \(\ell\) and each \(f\) with \(q_f^\ell>0\), the strict-cycle lemma supplies an open cube \(B_{\ell f}\) contained in the response patch for \(f\).  Let \(G_\ell\) be the absolutely continuous probability law that assigns mass \(q_f^\ell\) uniformly on \(B_{\ell f}\).  Choose distinct constants \(c_\ell\), put
\[
 \lambda^\ell=(c_\ell,\ldots,c_\ell)\in\mathbb R^J,
\]
and give \(\lambda\) the mass \(\omega_\ell\) at \(\lambda^\ell\).  Conditional on \(\lambda=\lambda^\ell\), draw \(\epsilon_1\) and \(\epsilon_2\) independently from the translate of \(G_\ell\) by \(-\lambda^\ell\).  Both conditional shock laws are identical and absolutely continuous, while \(\lambda^\ell+\epsilon_t\sim G_\ell\).  Therefore their response-table law is exactly \(q^\ell\), and the conditional path table is \(v(q^\ell)\).  Mixing over \(\ell\) produces exactly \(P\).  Every supported draw lies inside a strict patch, so maximizers are unique; zero cell probabilities and boundary points require no limit.  This proves sharpness with at most \(m\) fixed-effect types.

There are finitely many response tables and each finite comparison multigraph has finitely many directed simple cycles.  By the graph construction, every cycle weight is
\[
 W_C(\kappa)=A_C+B_C\kappa,
\]
with \(A_C\in\mathbb Q\) and integer \(B_C\).  Hence the set consisting of zero and all its nonnegative roots is finite, so \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{des}}\) and \(K=\max\mathcal B_{\mathrm{des}}\) are finite.

For \(\kappa>K\), an affine cycle weight is positive exactly in the following cases: \(B_C>0\); or \(B_C=0\) and \(A_C>0\).  Indeed, if \(B_C<0\), the weight is negative to the right of its root (and is already negative on the nonnegative half-line if that root is negative); if \(B_C>0\), it is positive to the right of its root (and is already positive if that root is negative).  Thus the strict-cycle lemma and the definition of \(F_\infty\) give
\[
 F_\kappa=F_\infty\qquad(\kappa>K).
\]
The sharp-body theorem therefore yields \(\mathcal C_\kappa=\mathcal C_\infty\) on the terminal stratum.

Suppose now that \(\Theta(P)\ne\varnothing\).  If \(P\in\mathcal C_\infty\), then \((K,+\infty)\subseteq\Theta(P)\), so \(U(P)=+\infty\).  If \(P\notin\mathcal C_\infty\), no \(\kappa>K\) is compatible, so the nonempty set \(\Theta(P)\) is bounded above and \(U(P)<+\infty\).  Compactness of \(\mathcal C_\infty\) gives
\[
 P\notin\mathcal C_\infty
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \inf_{Q\in\mathcal C_\infty}\|P-Q\|_\infty>0,
\]
which is the asserted criterion in terms of \(D_\infty(P)\).

It remains to establish the endpoint assertions.  If \(P\in\mathcal C_{\kappa_0}\), write it as a finite convex combination of \(v(q^\ell)\) as in the sharp-body theorem.  Only finitely many response tables have positive mass in these vectors.  Every cycle weight of each such table is strictly positive at \(\kappa_0\), hence remains positive in a relative neighborhood of \(\kappa_0\) in \([0,+\infty)\).  The same \(q^\ell\) and mixing weights therefore rationalize \(P\) throughout that neighborhood.  Consequently \(\Theta(P)\) is relatively open.

Removing the finite breakpoint set partitions \([0,+\infty)\) into finitely many open strata, and all cycle signs, hence \(F_\kappa\) and \(\mathcal C_\kappa\), are constant on each stratum.  It follows that \(\Theta(P)\) is a finite union of relatively open intervals.  A finite upper endpoint can occur only at a boundary of one of these strata, hence belongs to \(\mathcal B_{\mathrm{des}}\), and relative openness shows that it is not attained.

Finally, for a fixed response set \(F\), membership has the explicit finite semialgebraic form
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 w_\ell\ge0,\quad \sum_{\ell=1}^{m}w_\ell=1,
 \qquad q_{\ell f}\ge0,\quad \sum_{f\in F}q_{\ell f}=1,\\
 P_{ab}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}w_\ell
 \left(\sum_{f\in F}q_{\ell f}\mathbf 1\{f_1=a\}\right)
 \left(\sum_{f\in F}q_{\ell f}\mathbf 1\{f_2(a)=b\}\right)
 \quad(a\in M_1,b\in M_2).
 \end{gathered}
\]
The preceding bound of \(m\) components makes this a finite polynomial feasibility system.  Enumerating the breakpoint values, one representative of each open stratum, and the breakpoint bodies themselves, and deciding these systems therefore recovers all of \(\Theta(P)\) and its exact upper endpoint.  No monotonicity of \(\kappa\mapsto\mathcal C_\kappa\) is used.

Fix \(H\in\{F_\kappa,F_\infty\}\) and write \(N=|H|\).  These response sets are nonempty: at a finite price a generic \(z\), outside finitely many tie hyperplanes, induces a strict response table, and the terminal equality \(F_\kappa=F_\infty\) for \(\kappa>K\) gives the terminal case.  If \(N=1\), its simplex consists of one point, so \(\mathcal C_{H,L}=\mathcal C_H\) and \(e_{H,L}=0\).

Suppose \(N\ge2\), order the elements of \(H\), and take \(q\in\Delta(H)\).  For the first \(N-1\) coordinates put
\[
 q'_j=\frac{\lfloor Lq_j\rfloor}{L},
 \qquad
 q'_N=1-\sum_{j<N}q'_j.
\]
Then \(q'\in\mathcal G_{H,L}\) and
\[
 \|q-q'\|_1
 =2\sum_{j<N}(q_j-q'_j)
 \le\frac{2(N-1)}{L}.
\]
If \(x\) and \(x'\) are probability vectors, the mass they assign to any common subset differs by at most their total variation \(\|x-x'\|_1/2\).  Since both \(r_a\) and \(s_{ab}\) are probabilities of subsets of \(H\), with \(\Delta_q=\|q-q'\|_1\),
\[
 |r_a(q)-r_a(q')|\le\frac{\Delta_q}{2},
 \qquad
 |s_{ab}(q)-s_{ab}(q')|\le\frac{\Delta_q}{2}.
\]
All factors lie in \([0,1]\), and therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |v_{ab}(q)-v_{ab}(q')|
 &\le |r_a(q)-r_a(q')|s_{ab}(q)
      +r_a(q')|s_{ab}(q)-s_{ab}(q')|\\
 &\le\Delta_q
 \le\frac{2(N-1)}{L}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The left side is also at most one.  Hence \(\|v(q)-v(q')\|_\infty\le e_{H,L}\).

The grid image is a subset of the full image, so \(\mathcal C_{H,L}\subseteq\mathcal C_H\).  Conversely, if
\[
 Q=\sum_{j=1}^{s}\theta_jv(q^j)\in\mathcal C_H,
 \qquad \theta_j\ge0,
 \qquad \sum_j\theta_j=1,
\]
apply the preceding rounding separately to every \(q^j\), obtaining \(q^{j\prime}\in\mathcal G_{H,L}\).  Then \(Q_L=\sum_j\theta_jv(q^{j\prime})\in\mathcal C_{H,L}\) and
\[
 \|Q-Q_L\|_\infty
 \le\sum_j\theta_j\|v(q^j)-v(q^{j\prime})\|_\infty
 \le e_{H,L}.
\]
This proves the deterministic sandwich.

Both bodies are compact.  Inclusion gives
\[
 \operatorname{dist}_\infty(R,\mathcal C_H)
 \le d_{H,L}(R).
\]
For a nearest \(Q\in\mathcal C_H\), choose the preceding \(Q_L\); the triangle inequality yields
\[
 d_{H,L}(R)\le\|R-Q_L\|_\infty
 \le\operatorname{dist}_\infty(R,\mathcal C_H)+e_{H,L}.
\]
Rearranging and using nonnegativity proves
\[
 \max\{0,d_{H,L}(R)-e_{H,L}\}
 \le\operatorname{dist}_\infty(R,\mathcal C_H)
 \le d_{H,L}(R).
\]

For the certification claim, enumerate the finite grid image as rational vectors \(x^1,\ldots,x^G\).  When \(R\) is rational, \(d_{H,L}(R)\) is the value of the rational linear program
\[
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \text{minimize}&\delta\\
 \text{over}&\delta\ge0,\ \omega_g\ge0\\
 \text{subject to}&\displaystyle\sum_{g=1}^G\omega_g=1,\\
 &\displaystyle-\delta\le R_j-\sum_{g=1}^G\omega_gx^g_j\le\delta,
 \quad j=1,\ldots,m.
 \end{array}
\]
Its explicit dual is
\[
 \begin{array}{ll}
 \text{maximize}&u^\top R-t\\
 \text{over}&u=u^+-u^-,\quad u^+,u^-\ge0,\quad t\in\mathbb R\\
 \text{subject to}&\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^m(u_j^++u_j^-)\le1,\\
 &t\ge u^\top x^g,\quad g=1,\ldots,G.
 \end{array}
\]
For completeness, equality of these two values follows directly by eliminating \(\delta\) from the primal: \(\delta=\max_j|R_j-(\sum_g\omega_gx^g)_j|\); the supporting signed convex combination of the active coordinates gives \(u\), while minimization over \(\omega\) imposes \(t\ge u^\top x^g\).  Conversely every displayed dual feasible pair satisfies
\[
 u^\top R-t\le u^\top\left(R-\sum_g\omega_gx^g\right)
 \le\left\|R-\sum_g\omega_gx^g\right\|_\infty
\]
for every primal feasible \(\omega\), which is weak duality; the active-coordinate construction gives equality at a minimizing face.  All constraint matrices are rational.  Gaussian elimination on each of the finitely many candidate active sets therefore produces rational optimal primal and dual basic solutions, and direct substitution certifies feasibility and equality.  Stopping earlier after finding feasible primal and dual values within any prescribed positive rational gap gives rational numbers \(d^-\le d_{H,L}(R)\le d^+\).

With \(L_n=n\), \(\eta_n=1/n\), and \(R=\widehat P\), which is rational, the stipulated certificates satisfy
\[
 d^-_{H,n}\le d_{H,L_n}(\widehat P),
 \qquad d^+_{H,n}-d^-_{H,n}\le\eta_n.
\]
The deterministic distance inequality thus gives
\[
 \underline D_{H,n}
 =\max\{0,d^-_{H,n}-e_{H,L_n}\}
 \le\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\widehat P,\mathcal C_H).
\]
Finally \(e_{H,L}\to0\) for fixed finite \(H\), and the primal--dual gap may be made arbitrarily small.  Choosing each below half of a requested positive tolerance certifies the requested distance precision.

For a path cell \(j=(a,b)\), the variables \(X_{ij}=\mathbf 1\{Y_{i1}=a,Y_{i2}=b\}\) are iid Bernoulli with mean \(P_j\).  For a Bernoulli variable \(X\) with mean \(p\), elementary differentiation of
\[
 \log\mathbb E\exp\{s(X-p)\}=-sp+\log(1-p+pe^s)
\]
gives the uniform bound \(\log\mathbb E e^{s(X-p)}\le s^2/8\).  Applying Markov's inequality to the exponential and minimizing over \(s>0\) gives
\[
 \Pr\{\widehat P_j-P_j\ge x\}\le e^{-2nx^2},
 \qquad
 \Pr\{P_j-\widehat P_j\ge x\}\le e^{-2nx^2}.
\]
The union bound over the \(m\) path cells therefore yields, for
\(\rho_{n,\alpha}=\sqrt{\log(2m/\alpha)/(2n)}\),
\[
 \Pr\left\{\|\widehat P-P\|_\infty\le\rho_{n,\alpha}\right\}
 \ge1-2m e^{-2n\rho_{n,\alpha}^2}=1-\alpha.
\]
This inequality contains no unknown feature of the maintained law, so it is uniform over that law.

Let \(E_n\) denote this single simultaneous event.  If \(\kappa\in\Theta(P)\), then \(P\in\mathcal C_H\) for the response set \(H\) assigned by the construction to the open stratum or breakpoint containing \(\kappa\).  On \(E_n\),
\[
 \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\widehat P,\mathcal C_H)
 \le\|\widehat P-P\|_\infty
 \le\rho_{n,\alpha}.
\]
The certified-approximation theorem gives
\[
 \underline D_{H,n}le
 \operatorname{dist}_\infty(\widehat P,\mathcal C_H)
 \le\rho_{n,\alpha},
\]
so the construction retains that entire stratum or that breakpoint.  The same argument applies when \(\kappa>K\), because then \(H=F_\infty\).  Consequently
\[
 E_n\subseteq\{\Theta(P)\subseteq\widehat\Theta_{n,\alpha}\},
\]
and the preceding probability bound proves whole-set coverage.  There is no union over values of \(\kappa\): every retention conclusion is made on the same event \(E_n\).  By definition of the reported region, retaining the separately tested terminal stratum includes all of \((K,+\infty)\), so its reported upper endpoint is \(+\infty\).

For consistency, put \(\delta=D_\infty(P)>0\) and \(N_\infty=|F_\infty|<\infty\).  The optimization-gap inequalities imply
\[
 d^-_{F_\infty,n}
 \ge d_{\infty,L_n}(\widehat P)-\eta_n.
\]
Because \(\mathcal C_{\infty,L_n}\subseteq\mathcal C_\infty\), the reverse triangle inequality gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \underline D_{F_\infty,n}
 &\ge d_{\infty,L_n}(\widehat P)-\eta_n-e_{F_\infty,L_n}\\
 &\ge\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\widehat P,\mathcal C_\infty)
       -\eta_n-e_{F_\infty,L_n}\\
 &\ge\delta-\|\widehat P-P\|_\infty
       -\eta_n-e_{F_\infty,L_n}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here the first inequality remains valid when its right side is negative because \(\underline D_{F_\infty,n}\ge0\).  Now \(\eta_n=1/n\to0\), \(e_{F_\infty,L_n}\le2(N_\infty-1)/n\to0\), \(\rho_{n,\alpha}\to0\), and the same exponential bound shows \(\|\widehat P-P\|_\infty\to0\) in probability.  Hence
\[
 \Pr\{\underline D_{F_\infty,n}>\rho_{n,\alpha}\}\longrightarrow1.
\]
The terminal stratum is then rejected, and the remaining finitely many retained pieces lie in \([0,K]\), so the declared upper endpoint is finite with probability tending to one.  No conclusion of this kind is used or claimed when \(D_\infty(P)=0\).

Assume first that \(M_1=M_2\), and fix \(d'\in A\).  Subtracting the period-specific constants common to all alternatives, define
\[
 g_{1d}=-p_{1d}-\mathbf 1\{h_0\ne d\}\kappa,
 \qquad
 g_{2d}(d')=-p_{2d}-\mathbf 1\{d'\ne d\}\kappa,
 \qquad
 \Delta_d(d')=g_{2d}(d')-g_{1d}.
\]
The displayed premise in the proposition says exactly that
\[
 \Delta_d(d')\ge\Delta_c(d')
 \quad\text{for every }d\in A, c\in M_1\setminus A.
\]
For a fixed shock vector \(z\), suppose the first-period unique maximizer \(d\) lies in \(A\).  For every \(c\notin A\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 [g_{2d}(d')+z_d]-[g_{2c}(d')+z_c]
 &=[g_{1d}+z_d-(g_{1c}+z_c)]
   +[\Delta_d(d')-\Delta_c(d')]\\
 &>0.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus, using the same \(z\), period-two choice under lag \(d'\) must also lie in \(A\).  Conditional on \(\lambda\), let \(q_A(\lambda)\) be the probability that a one-period draw makes the period-one choice lie in \(A\).  Conditional homogeneity, independence, and the preceding samplewise containment imply, for every \(d'\in A\),
\[
 \Pr(Y_2\in A\mid Y_1=d',\lambda)\ge q_A(\lambda).
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \Pr(Y_1\in A,Y_2\in A\mid\lambda)
 &=\sum_{d'\in A}\Pr(Y_1=d'\mid\lambda)
       \Pr(Y_2\in A\mid Y_1=d',\lambda)\\
 &\ge q_A(\lambda)^2.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Integration and the identity
\(\mathbb E[q_A^2]-(\mathbb E q_A)^2
=\mathbb E[(q_A-\mathbb E q_A)^2]\ge0\)
give
\[
 \Pr(Y_1\in A,Y_2\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)
 \ge\Pr(Y_1\in A\mid Y_0=h_0)^2.
\]
If the right marginal is positive, division gives the ratio form; if it is zero, that conditional ratio need not be defined.  When \(A=M_1\), both sides equal one.  With changing menus, the displayed common-menu premise is not well typed for one common inside--outside partition: an entrant or exiting alternative lacks one of the two comparisons used in the equality above.  Hence the samplewise containment argument does not apply directly to the full changing menus.

For any response table \(f\), the strict-cycle lemma and the definition of \(I_f\) give
\[
 f\in F_\kappa\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\kappa\in I_f.
\]
Because \(I_f\) is the intersection of finitely many strict affine inequalities \(A_C+B_C\kappa>0\), it is unbounded above if and only if no inequality supplies a finite upper bound; equivalently, it then contains \((k_f,+\infty)\) for some finite \(k_f\).  By the definition of terminal feasibility, this is equivalent to \(f\in F_\infty\).  Therefore every table feasible at some finite price is terminal-feasible exactly when every \(I_f\) is empty or unbounded above.  Under this response-type condition \(F_\kappa\subseteq F_\infty\) for every \(\kappa\), whence
\[
 \mathcal C_\kappa\subseteq\mathcal C_\infty.
\]
If \(P\) is rationalizable, it belongs to some \(\mathcal C_\kappa\), hence to \(\mathcal C_\infty\); the terminal-frontier theorem then gives \(U(P)=+\infty\).

Finally consider the stated pure-entry response table.  Period-one choice of \(b\) over \(a\) is
\[
 z_a-z_b<p_{1a}-p_{1b}-\kappa.
\]
Period-two choice of \(a\) after lag \(a\), and choice of \(b\) after lag \(b\), respectively require
\[
 p_{2a}-p_{2b}-\kappa<z_a-z_b,
 \qquad
 z_a-z_b<p_{2a}-p_{2b}+\kappa.
\]
The intersection is nonempty exactly when
\[
 (p_{1a}-p_{1b})-(p_{2a}-p_{2b})=\tau>0
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 2\kappa>0.
\]
The entrant \(c\) is never designated as a winner, and all comparisons against it are satisfied simultaneously by choosing \(z_c\) sufficiently small.  Thus \(f\in F_\kappa\) exactly when \(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa>0\).  Strictness excludes both the zero-sign case and the threshold \(\kappa=0\).  If a menu is a singleton, or a comparison graph has no edge, the corresponding choice is forced and the compatible body reduces to the appropriate degenerate probability simplex, as the definitions assert.

open_obligations.what_is_open: The unresolved step is the complete latent-free projection for negative entry with both off-diagonal probabilities positive, the zero-sign entry body, and all six exit bodies, including every equality and zero-probability boundary and an explicit attaining mixture in each regime.
open_obligations.obstruction: The exact negative-entry cone has eight coupled quadratic curve families sharing the same four square-coordinate budgets. When both off-diagonal coordinates are positive, their allocation constraints do not separate: the dual support function has an active switching term involving the smaller off-diagonal mass. Optimizing the face inequalities separately therefore supplies only an outer description, not the necessary-and-sufficient Boolean formula demanded by the open-ended question. No frozen assumption or established result eliminates these coupled allocations, and treating a generic quantifier-elimination output as the requested analytic formula is expressly excluded.
open_obligations.attempted: The response tables were enumerated by strict-cycle tests for all nine terminal classes. The binary-first-menu reduction was used to enumerate all twenty two-patch curves. Pure rays were removed, the remaining negative-entry and zero-sign cones were reduced to eight and seven nonredundant quadratic curve families, respectively, and the dual minimization over the two off-diagonal coefficients was carried out. Positive-sign entry and the two informative negative-sign boundary faces were eliminated constructively. The remaining route is a finite active-allocation case split for the joint positive-off-diagonal regime, followed by comparison of every resulting support value with exact quadratic maximization over the twenty curves, and then the analogous three-first-choice allocation for exit.
open_obligations.partial_result:
Relabel the continuing plans \(a,b\), write the path table as
\[
 (A,B,C,R,S,T)=(P_{aa},P_{ab},P_{ac},P_{ba},P_{bb},P_{bc}),
 \]
and put \(\tau=(p_{1a}-p_{1b})-(p_{2a}-p_{2b})\).  Exact strict-cycle enumeration gives the terminal entry response tables
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
&f_1=a&f_1=b\\ \hline
\tau<0&aaa,aab,aac,acc&bab,bac,bbb,bcb,bcc\\
\tau=0&aaa,aac,acc&bab,bac,bbb,bcb,bcc\\
\tau>0&aaa,aac,acc&baa,bab,bac,bbb,bcb,bcc.
\end{array}
\]
For exit, write the lag-choice words
\[
 L_0=bbb,
 \quad L_1=abb,
 \quad L_2=aba,
 \quad L_3=aaa.
\]
The exact permitted indices for first choices \(a,b,c\), in that order, are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{initial status}&\operatorname{sign}(\tau)&a&b&c\\ \hline
b\text{ continues}&-&\{2,3\}&\{0,1,2\}&\{0,1,2,3\}\\
b\text{ continues}&0&\{3\}&\{0,1,2\}&\{0,1,2,3\}\\
b\text{ continues}&+&\{3\}&\{0,1,2,3\}&\{0,1,2,3\}\\
c\text{ exits}&-&\{1,2,3\}&\{0,1\}&\{0,1,2,3\}\\
c\text{ exits}&0&\{2,3\}&\{0,1\}&\{0,1,2,3\}\\
c\text{ exits}&+&\{2,3\}&\{0,1,2\}&\{0,1,2,3\}.
\end{array}
\]
Each listed patch is open and nonempty by its strict comparison inequalities.

For positive-sign entry define, for nonnegative \(a,c,s,h,b\),
\[
 \Phi(a,c,s,h;b)=
 \bigl[bc\le h(a+c)\ \wedge\ b^2\le s(a+c)\bigr]
 \ \vee\ 
 \bigl[bc>h(a+c)\ \wedge\ c(b-h)^2+ah^2\le sac\bigr].
\]
Then the complete constructive result already obtained is
\[
 P\in\mathcal C_\infty
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 B\le R+T\ \wedge\ \Phi(A,C,S,T;B)
 \qquad(\tau>0).
\]
It includes all zero boundaries without division.  For negative-sign entry, two complete faces are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 R=0:\quad&P\in\mathcal C_\infty
 \Longleftrightarrow
 S\ge L\ \wedge\ \Phi(A,C,S-L,H;B),\\
 &L=\max\{0,B-T\},\qquad H=\min\{B,T\};\\[2mm]
 B=0:\quad&P\in\mathcal C_\infty
 \Longleftrightarrow
 A\ge L\ \wedge\ R^2\le(A-L)(S+T),\\
 &L=\max\{0,R-C\}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The maxima and minima expand into two polynomial branches and the proofs allocate rank-one curve masses explicitly, so these are finite Boolean formulas with constructive attainability.

The full negative-entry cone is exactly the cone generated by the four pure rays in coordinates \(A,C,S,T\) and, for \(s,t\ge0\), the eight curves
\[
\begin{array}{l}
(s^2+st,0,0,st,t^2,0),\\
(s^2+st,0,0,st,0,t^2),\\
(s^2,st,0,st,t^2,0),\\
(s^2,0,st,st,t^2,0),\\
(s^2,0,st,st,0,t^2),\\
(s^2,st,0,0,t^2+st,0),\\
(s^2,st,0,0,t^2,st),\\
(0,st,s^2,0,t^2,st).
\end{array}
\]
The zero-sign cone removes the sixth curve.  Thus this reduction is already finite and exact, not an infinite-dimensional residual.  If \(a,c,s,t\ge0\) are dual coefficients on the four pure-ray coordinates and \(b,r\) are the coefficients on \(B,R\), exact nonnegativity on these curves is equivalent to
\[
 r\ge-\rho,
 \qquad b\ge-\beta,
 \qquad b+r\ge-\gamma,
\]
where
\[
 \rho=\min(a,c)+2\sqrt{a\min(s,t)},
 \qquad
 \beta=\min\{s+2\sqrt{as},t+2\sqrt{as},t+2\sqrt{cs}\},
 \qquad
 \gamma=2\sqrt{as}.
\]
For fixed \(a,c,s,t\), minimizing the dual objective over \(b,r\) gives
\[
 -\left[B\beta+R\rho-\min(B,R)\max\{\beta+\rho-\gamma,0\}\right].
\]
The last coupled term proves exactly why the two solved faces cannot simply be intersected to characterize the positive-off-diagonal regime, and it is the computable starting point for the required kill test.
